Study 01 · Woodland Hills Topanga Willows: shade for a block that faces the afternoon sun A strip center with its storefronts facing west and a parking lot with one tree in it. Seven moves that keep the lot working and put most of it in shade. 17 new trees on the property 68 → 61 parking stalls 31 linked sources Read the study → Study 02 [NEXT SITE: a school quad or campus edge with no shade] Planned Study 03 [NEXT SITE: a stretch of street or a bus stop] Planned Method Four steps, in this order The order matters. The drawing comes second, and the proposal comes last. 1 Read the site Walk it, photograph it at the hottest hour, and draw what is really there in plan: the building, the stalls, the driveways, the trees. 2 Find the evidence Measured results only: government data, peer-reviewed studies and the city’s own code. Anything I cannot verify gets flagged. 3 Draw the fix A plan, a section and a detail that fit the site as it is. Then count what it costs, like parking stalls given up. 4 Say what is unknown Every study ends with its limits and with the numbers I would measure before and after to know whether it worked. Notes From the notebook Short pieces on what each study taught me. More as the studies come. The first plan I had for Topanga Willows was wrong. It showed the building at the back of the lot with parking in front, because that is what a strip center usually looks like. The aerial photo says otherwise. The building sits right on the sidewalk and all the parking is behind it. That one fact changed the whole argument: the storefronts face west into the afternoon sun, and the building only shades the first row of cars. Draw what is there before you draw what you want. The site had the answer. More notes → About I care about what happens between buildings I am Nathan, a student in the west San Fernando Valley, headed toward construction management. Redrawn Valley is where I practice the whole job on real places: reading a site, checking the rules, drawing the fix and being honest about the cost. h: Applying it to a parking lot#
pages.x: Bioswale | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Water and ground Bioswale A planted channel that slows, filters and soaks in street runoff Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~1 min Sources 3 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Bioswale A swale takes in curb runoff. Concept sketch. Type Green infrastructure Related term Rain garden, bioretention [1] Valley example Elmer Avenue, Sun Valley [2] Reported capacity 24 swales treat 115,000 gal [2] Related Permeable paving Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is Case: Elmer Avenue Applying it to a parking lot See also Notes What it is # A bioswale is a shallow planted channel or bed that takes in runoff from a road, roof or lot and lets it soak into the ground. It is a close relative of the rain garden. The EPA describes a rain garden as a depressed area in the landscape that collects rain from a roof, driveway or street and lets it soak in, planted with grasses and flowering perennials. It can also filter pollutants and shelter wildlife. More complex versions with drainage systems and amended soils are often called bioretention. [1] Case: Elmer Avenue # Elmer Avenue in Sun Valley was a street with no pedestrian or stormwater infrastructure and frequent flooding. The retrofit captures and filters runoff from a 40-acre area. [2] The project reports: 24 bioswales that together can capture and treat 115,000 gallons of runoff and add 1,728 square feet of planting. Up to 5.4 million gallons of stormwater infiltrated per year, and reduced lead, copper and suspended solids concentrations by 60%, 33% and 18%. 23 native trees along the sidewalks. Residents satisfied with the block’s walkability rising from under 2% of survey respondents in 2006 to 92% in 2011. Those are figures reported by the project’s case study brief, not independent audits. The survey is also small and self-reported. [2] Applying it to a parking lot # In my Topanga Willows study I turn the strip where car noses overhang at the edge of a lot into a swale, with curb cuts that let runoff in. [3] That is a concept, drawn from a street-scale precedent: Elmer Avenue is a residential street, not a retail lot, and I do not know how the soil under any Woodland Hills lot drains. A percolation test would come before any design is real. pages.x: Cool pavement | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Heat Cool pavement Paving made to stay cooler than conventional asphalt Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~1 min Sources 3 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Cool pavement Surface temperature is not comfort. Concept sketch. Type Paving strategy Mechanisms Reflect more sun, evaporate water, or both [1] Arizona pilot Asphalt up to 152°F; cool pavement 10–16°F cooler [1] LA program 175+ lane miles [2] Main caution Can feel hotter to pedestrians [2] Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is Los Angeles’s experience My working rule What I do not know See also Notes What it is # The EPA uses cool pavement for paving materials that reflect more solar energy, enhance water evaporation, or have otherwise been modified to stay cooler than conventional pavements. It can be made with ordinary asphalt and concrete, with coatings, or with grass paving. [1] A pilot study in Arizona found conventional paving such as asphalt reaching surface temperatures up to 152°F at midday, while cool pavements stayed 10 to 16°F cooler. [1] Los Angeles’s experience # Los Angeles has spent millions installing “cool” pavement on more than 175 lane miles across the city. [2] But a UCLA study discussed by NBC Los Angeles says more research is needed to know the real benefits: cool pavement may lower surface temperatures yet feel hotter to a person, in part because the effect of sunlight is increased as heat re-radiates from the pavement. [2] I read that as a lesson in what to measure. Surface temperature is easy to read with a thermometer; comfort depends on air temperature, wind, humidity and radiation from every surface around a person. My working rule # This is my design judgment, not a sourced finding: shade first, and use reflective coatings only where people are not standing, such as drive aisles. My Topanga Willows study follows that order. [3] What I do not know # Limits of this entry I read the UCLA findings through a news report, not the report itself, so I state them at the level of detail the report gave. The Arizona figures are from one pilot, not a Los Angeles measurement. pages.d: Roofs, roads and parking lots that shed water instead of absorbing it, and what that does to floods and creeks.
pages.x: Impervious surface | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Water and ground Impervious surface Any hard cover that rain cannot soak through Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~1 min Sources 4 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Impervious surface Rain on hard cover runs off. Concept sketch. Type Land-cover category Examples Roofs, roads, driveways, parking lots Effect More runoff, less infiltration [1] Linked risk More frequent, more severe floods [1] Fixes Bioswales , permeable paving Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is What happens to the water The heat link In the Valley What I do not know See also Notes What it is # An impervious surface is one that rain cannot pass through. The USGS gives the everyday examples: superhighways, streets, pavement, driveways and house roofs. [1] Land that is natural or planted can take in rain; hard cover sends it somewhere else. What happens to the water # In a forested watershed a significant share of rainfall is absorbed into the soil, stored as groundwater and released slowly to streams. When a watershed urbanizes and vegetation is replaced by impervious cover, there is less area where rain can infiltrate, so more runoff has to be collected by curbs, storm sewers and ditches and carried straight to streams. In a developed watershed much more water reaches a stream much more quickly, and the USGS states that severe flood events happen more often as impervious area grows. [1] The heat link # Impervious cover is also hard and dry, which is why it appears in the EPA’s list of heat island causes: hard, dry surfaces provide less shade and moisture than natural landscapes. [2] A parking lot is both problems at once, which is why I treat permeable paving and bioswales as part of the cooling design and not only the drainage design. In the Valley # Two Valley projects show the other direction. On Elmer Avenue in Sun Valley, a street with no pedestrian or stormwater infrastructure and frequent flooding was retrofitted so that bioswales and a buried infiltration gallery capture runoff from a 40-acre area. [3] The Tujunga Wash, a 13-mile tributary of the Los Angeles River, was channelized for flood control in the 1950s; [4] see riparian corridor for the greenway built beside it. What I do not know # Limits of this entry I do not have a percent-impervious figure for the Valley or for any site I have studied. For a site, I estimate it from aerial imagery, and I label it as an estimate. pages.x: Los Angeles River | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Water and ground Los Angeles River The channelized river that begins in the western San Fernando Valley Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~1 min Sources 4 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Los Angeles River Headwaters to the Basin. Concept sketch. Type River, mostly channelized Source Confluence of Bell Creek and Arroyo Calabasas, Canoga Park [1] Length About 51 miles to Long Beach [1] Watershed About 827 sq mi [1] Valley parts Sepulveda Basin, Tujunga Wash [2] Related Riparian corridor Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents Where it starts The river in the Valley Why it matters to a small place What I do not know See also Notes Where it starts # The Los Angeles River’s official beginning is the confluence of two channelized streams, Bell Creek and Arroyo Calabasas, in the Canoga Park part of Los Angeles, just east of State Route 27, which is Topanga Canyon Boulevard. [1] From there it flows about 51 miles through the San Fernando Valley, downtown Los Angeles and the Gateway Cities to San Pedro Bay at Long Beach, draining a watershed of about 827 square miles. [1] My first study site is on that same boulevard, though I have not traced where its runoff goes. The river in the Valley # The Sepulveda Basin is a flood-control basin and, with the Griffith Park area and the Willow Avenue estuary in Long Beach, one of only three stretches with a soft bottom. [2] The Tujunga Wash is a 13-mile urban tributary that was channelized for flood control in the 1950s. [3] Why it matters to a small place # Most of the river is a concrete channel designed to move floodwater out quickly, which is the same logic as a storm drain on a parking lot (see impervious surface ). The revitalization office reports that only the Sepulveda Basin and the Glendale Narrows presently support riparian habitat in the 32-mile project area. [4] A site that holds water and plants native trees is a small version of what the river lost (see riparian corridor ). What I do not know # Limits of this entry Length and basin size come from Wikipedia, which I use only for basic geography. I have not confirmed the 51-mile and 827-square-mile figures against a primary source, such as the Army Corps of Engineers or the county, so treat them as approximate. h: Where I have seen it used#
pages.x: Permeable paving | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Water and ground Permeable paving Pavement that lets rain pass through to the ground below Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~1 min Sources 4 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Permeable paving Rain passes through to a gravel base. Concept sketch. Type Paving system Kinds Pervious asphalt, pervious concrete, interlocking pavers, plastic grid pavers [1] Main benefit Less runoff, some filtering [1] Valley example Elmer Avenue, Sun Valley [2] Related Bioswale Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is Where I have seen it used Heat is a separate question A design judgment, labeled See also Notes What it is # Permeable paving is a family of surfaces that let rain and snowmelt seep through to underlying layers of soil and gravel. The EPA lists pervious asphalt, pervious concrete, interlocking pavers and plastic grid pavers. Besides cutting runoff, permeable pavements can filter pollutants and, by reducing the need for some conventional drainage features, reduce construction costs for residential and commercial development. [1] Where I have seen it used # The Elmer Avenue retrofit in Sun Valley installed 63 square feet of permeable concrete and 1,560 square feet of permeable pavers, alongside its bioswales. [2] Heat is a separate question # The EPA groups permeable surfaces under “cool pavements” because they can stay cooler by letting water evaporate. [3] But the cooling depends on moisture, and in a dry Valley summer I do not know how much of it is there. I treat permeable paving as a water measure first and a possible heat bonus second. For surface heat, see cool pavement . A design judgment, labeled # In my Topanga Willows study I put pavers under the parked stalls but keep asphalt in the drive aisles. That is my judgment about turning loads, not a rule I found in a source, [4] and it is the kind of detail an engineer would have to confirm. Permeable systems also need upkeep to stay open, and I have no cost or maintenance figures for Los Angeles. pages.d: The habitat along water, how much of Los Angeles’s was lost, and the Valley places where it survives.
pages.x: Riparian corridor | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Water and ground Riparian corridor The strip of living habitat along a stream or river Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~1 min Sources 4 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Riparian corridor A bank with and without a planted edge. Concept sketch. Type Habitat and landscape type Where, in LA Sepulveda Basin; Glendale Narrows [1] Loss, LA River 90–95% of in-stream riparian habitat [1] Valley example Tujunga Wash Greenway, 15 acres [2] Related Los Angeles River Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is What was lost Sepulveda Basin Tujunga Wash Greenway Why a small site cares See also Notes What it is # A riparian corridor is the band of plants, soil and wildlife habitat beside a stream. Before the Los Angeles River was channelized, the areas next to it were riparian ecosystems with many native plant and animal species. [3] What was lost # The City of Los Angeles’s river revitalization office cites the California Coastal Conservancy: close to 100% of the original wetlands and 90–95% of in-stream riparian habitat in the Los Angeles River watershed have been lost to urbanization and channelization. Within the 32-mile river project area, the only places that currently support riparian habitat are the Sepulveda Basin and the Glendale Narrows, and both are stressed by exotic species, changed hydrology, dumped trash and encroaching development. [1] Sepulveda Basin # The Sepulveda Basin in the Valley is one of three places along the river with a soft bottom, and native willows dominate the banks between Burbank and Balboa Boulevards, though some non-native trees such as eucalyptus tower over the lower native shrubs. [4] The basin is also a flood-control basin, so the habitat and the engineering share the same ground. Tujunga Wash Greenway # A built example: the 1.2-mile Tujunga Wash Greenway turned an inaccessible right-of-way along a concrete flood channel into 15 acres of riparian habitat, 50 to 60 feet wide, planted with 1,100 trees and 18,000 shrubs and vines, all California natives. A naturalized streambed is fed by up to 325,000 gallons a day diverted from the channel. The project reports it infiltrates up to 118 million gallons of water a year from the channel, recharging the San Fernando groundwater basin, and cuts potential landscape water use by 70–80% by using native plants. [2] These are the project team’s reported figures from a case study brief, not independent measurements. Why a small site cares # My studies are not on river banks. But the Valley’s streets and lots drain toward these channels, so what I do with rain on a parking lot is the first link of the same system. See bioswale and impervious surface . pages.x: San Fernando Valley | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Valley context San Fernando Valley The inland basin north of the Santa Monica Mountains where my studies are set Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~1 min Sources 5 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . San Fernando Valley A bowl ringed by mountains. Concept sketch. Type Urbanized valley, Los Angeles County Area About 260 sq mi [1] Population About 1.8 million (2023) [1] Record heat 121°F, Pierce College, Sept. 6, 2020 [2] Ringed by Santa Susana, Simi Hills, Santa Monica, Verdugo, San Gabriel ranges [1] Studies Heat , canopy Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents The setting Why it runs hot Water and ground Studies here What I do not know See also Notes The setting # The San Fernando Valley, “the Valley” locally, is an urbanized valley in Los Angeles County, north of the Los Angeles Basin. It covers about 260 square miles and had about 1.8 million people in 2023. It is bounded by the Santa Susana Mountains to the northwest, the Simi Hills to the west, the Santa Monica Mountains to the south, the Verdugo Mountains to the east and the San Gabriel Mountains to the northeast. [1] It includes a large part of the City of Los Angeles plus Burbank, Calabasas, Glendale, Hidden Hills, San Fernando and several unincorporated areas. [1] Why it runs hot # Because of its relatively inland position and other factors, summer days in the Valley are typically hotter, and winter nights colder, than in the Los Angeles Basin. [1] The extreme is Woodland Hills: on Sept. 6, 2020 the official site at Pierce College reached 121°F, the highest temperature ever recorded at an official station in Los Angeles County; it was reached at about 1:30 p.m. [2] [3] That is a single day, and a record at one station, but it is the reason I picked this part of the city. The mechanics of why built-up places stay hotter are in urban heat island . Water and ground # The Valley holds the headwaters and a long reach of the Los Angeles River , with tributaries such as the Tujunga Wash, and some of the clearest examples of retrofitting hard ground to take rain, such as the Elmer Avenue project in Sun Valley. [4] Studies here # My first study is a shopping center in Woodland Hills: Topanga Willows . [5] What I do not know # Limits of this entry The area, population and mountain boundaries come from Wikipedia, which I use for basic geography only. The Valley is not one climate: temperatures vary by neighborhood and elevation, and I have not compared stations. pages.d: Who has shade and who does not in Los Angeles, and what the research says about fixing it.
pages.x: Shade equity | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Trees and shade Shade equity Equal access to the cooling benefits of tree cover Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~2 min Sources 5 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Shade equity Same street length, two kinds of walk. Concept sketch. Type Planning concept Definition Equal access to the cooling benefits of tree cover [1] Facets Distributional, recognitional, procedural Tools Tree Equity Score, canopy maps Related Tree canopy Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is What the evidence shows Three kinds of fairness What I do not know See also Notes What it is # Shade equity is equal access to the cooling benefits of tree cover. [1] The idea is that shade is not a luxury: on a hot day it is the difference between a walk to the bus that is tolerable and one that is not, and it is spread unevenly. What the evidence shows # In Los Angeles, TreePeople’s canopy report found that much of the city’s canopy is “not where the people are,” and that some residents live virtually in a forest while many others live in virtually treeless environments. [2] The national picture is similar. The National Equity Atlas reports that across racial and ethnic groups in urban areas, people living below the federal poverty level have lower tree canopy coverage than those above it. [3] American Forests built the Tree Equity Score to prioritize investment where need is greatest. [4] A 2025 study modeled street trees in one low-income and one high-income Los Angeles neighborhood under two sets of spacing guidelines. Structural differences such as parcel size, intersection density and street width limited how many trees each neighborhood could host. Looser guidelines narrowed the gap in tree numbers , but substantial gaps remained in tree stature, a proxy for canopy. The authors conclude that shade equity may be hard to fix by changing guidelines alone. [5] Three kinds of fairness # The Union of Concerned Scientists argues that growing shade should account for more than where trees physically stand. Distributional equity is the map of who has trees. Recognitional equity means understanding the conditions and root causes, and engaging residents about their own goals and concerns. Procedural equity means transparent decisions and fair access to them. [1] I take that last point seriously for my own work. My studies are drawn from aerial imagery and public research, and they are concept studies. They are not a substitute for asking the people who use a place what they need from it. What I do not know # Limits of this entry The UCS piece is an advocacy-science blog post, and I read the Tree Equity Score and National Equity Atlas pages only as summaries. I have not checked the Valley’s shade distribution myself. The Messier study covers two neighborhoods, so I treat it as a case, not a rule. pages.d: The underground half of tree planting: a published guideline, the Walt Disney World parking lot study, and a worked example.
pages.x: Soil volume | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Trees and shade Soil volume How much root-friendly ground a tree gets, and why that decides whether lot trees live Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~1 min Sources 2 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Soil volume A tree is half underground. Concept sketch. Type Planting design measure Guideline 2–3 cu ft of soil per 1 sq ft of crown spread [1] Field result Every tree with ≥1,500 cu ft was in good condition [2] Sample 1,127 trees, Walt Disney World [2] Related Tree canopy Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is A published guideline A field test What I do not know See also Notes What it is # Soil volume is the amount of uncompacted soil a tree’s roots can reach. In a parking lot it is the problem: a tree in a small paved island is, in the words of a Virginia Tech fact sheet, in a kind of pseudo-container. [1] A published guideline # The Virginia Tech fact sheet advises designing lot islands with as much soil volume as possible, ideally letting roots grow at least to the drip line, the edge of the crown, at maturity. It recommends 2 to 3 cubic feet of soil per 1 square foot of crown spread. [1] Worked example (my arithmetic) Take a tree whose mature crown is 30 feet across. The crown covers about π × 15² ≈ 707 square feet. At 2–3 cubic feet per square foot, that is about 1,400 to 2,100 cubic feet of soil, or a bed 3 feet deep and about 470 to 700 square feet. That is more than many parking islands provide, which is why soil, not the tree, is the hard part. A field test # A study of 1,127 parking lot trees at Walt Disney World found 81% in good condition and only 3% dead since planting, and that every tree in at least 1,500 cubic feet of soil was in good condition. Live oaks ( Quercus virginiana ) planted in groups did better than those planted singly. The authors also say existing planting recommendations were only imperfectly applicable to the site. [2] What I do not know # Limits of this entry The Disney lots are in Florida with different soil, species and irrigation than a Woodland Hills lot, and the 1,500 cubic feet result is for that sample. I do not know the soil under any Valley lot I have studied. A site would need a soil test and an arborist before I put numbers on a tree. pages.d: What “percent canopy” measures, Los Angeles’s numbers, and why canopy is not the same as shade on a sidewalk.
h: Canopy is not the same as shade#
pages.x: Tree canopy | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Trees and shade Tree canopy The share of ground covered by tree leaves and branches, seen from above Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~2 min Sources 2 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Tree canopy Canopy is the view from above. Concept sketch. Type Land-cover measure Unit Percent of land under tree crowns LA County About 18% [1] City of LA About 25% [1] Data year Circa 2016 Related Shade equity , soil volume Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is It is not spread evenly Canopy is not the same as shade What I do not know See also Notes What it is # Tree canopy is the layer of leaves, branches and stems that cover the ground when you look straight down. “Percent canopy” is the share of an area under that layer. It is the standard way cities count their urban forest because it can be estimated from aerial imagery instead of counted tree by tree. An analysis of land cover data from about 2016 found that 18% of Los Angeles County and 25% of the City of Los Angeles was covered by tree canopy. [1] That 25% is the number I cite for the city in my studies. It is not spread evenly # The same report found that five census block groups, one in Pacific Palisades, one in Los Feliz, two in Brentwood and one in Shadow Hills, hold 18% of the city’s total tree canopy while less than 1% of the city’s population lives there. [1] The authors point to a cause: more affluent residents can afford the hill areas, which are better suited to trees and less densely developed. [1] The Union of Concerned Scientists repeats the same pattern, nearly 20% of the urban forest where 1% of people live. [2] That unevenness is the subject of shade equity . Canopy is not the same as shade # This is my own reasoning, not a sourced finding: a percent canopy figure averages over an area, but a person stands at one spot. A neighborhood can have healthy canopy in back yards and none over its bus stops. And a young tree counts as a dot from above while casting almost no shade for years. When I plan planting on a site I therefore ask where the shade lands, at what hour, over what people are doing, and how big the tree will be when it is mature. Getting a tree to maturity in a paved lot depends mostly on what is underground, which is the subject of soil volume . What I do not know # Limits of this entry The 18% and 25% figures come from one 2016-era land cover analysis and will have changed. I do not have a canopy number for the Valley as a whole, for Woodland Hills, or for any block I have studied. I would need the county’s canopy layer clipped to a site to state one. pages.d: Why built-up places run hotter than their surroundings, and the five causes that matter on a parking lot.
pages.x: Urban heat island | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Heat Urban heat island Why built-up places run hotter than the land around them Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~3 min Sources 3 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Urban heat island Same sun, different surfaces. Concept sketch. Type Climate effect Also called UHI, heat island Size, U.S. Day: about 1–7°F warmer. Night: about 2–5°F warmer [1] Two kinds Surface and atmospheric Main levers Shade, vegetation, reflective surfaces, less paving Seen in San Fernando Valley Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is Five causes Surface and atmospheric Why it matters In the Valley What I do not know See also Notes What it is # An urban heat island is a city or neighborhood that is measurably warmer than the less built-up land around it. The U.S. EPA summarizes the research this way: in the United States, daytime temperatures in urban areas run about 1–7°F higher than in outlying areas, and nighttime temperatures about 2–5°F higher. [1] The gap is usually measured as a difference between a city and its surroundings, so it depends on which surroundings you pick. A heat island is not the same thing as a heat wave. A heat wave is weather. A heat island is a built-in offset that rides on top of the weather, and it is largest on the calm, clear days when the weather is already dangerous. [1] Five causes # The EPA lists five, and each one shows up on an ordinary parking lot: [1] Fewer natural landscapes. Trees, plants and water cool the air by shading, by releasing water from leaves, and by evaporation. Hard, dry surfaces such as roofs, sidewalks, roads and parking lots do less of all three. Material properties. Conventional pavement and roofing reflect less solar energy and absorb and emit more heat than vegetation. Heat islands often build through the day and become stronger after sunset as that stored heat leaks out slowly. Urban geometry. Tall buildings and narrow streets trap heat and block wind. Waste heat. Vehicles, air conditioners, buildings and industry all release heat. Weather and geography. Calm, clear weather makes heat islands worse. Wind and cloud cover suppress them. Nearby mountains can block wind or redirect it. The first two are the ones a small site can change. That is why my studies spend their effort on tree canopy and on what the ground is made of ( impervious surface , cool pavement ). Surface and atmospheric # The term covers two different measurements. A surface heat island is how hot the ground and roofs themselves get, which is what a satellite sees. The EPA notes that on a warm day conventional roofing can reach as much as 66°F warmer than the surrounding air. [1] An atmospheric heat island is the warmer air, which is what a thermometer in the shade reads. The EPA says atmospheric heat islands vary much less in intensity than surface ones. [1] This matters for design claims. A pavement that is 15°F cooler at the surface has not made the air 15°F cooler, and a person standing on it feels more than air temperature (see cool pavement ). Why it matters # The EPA ties heat islands to three costs. Electricity demand for air conditioning rises about 1–9% for each 2°F increase in temperature. Higher demand means more fossil-fuel emissions, and more sun and heat means more ground-level ozone. And hot weather contributes to heat-related illness and death, with older adults, young children, low-income populations, people who work outdoors and people with chronic conditions at greatest risk. From 2004 to 2018 the CDC recorded an average of 702 heat deaths per year in the U.S. [1] In the Valley # The Valley is a plausible heat island host: it is inland, ringed by mountains, and summer days there are typically hotter than in the Los Angeles Basin. [2] Its all-time county record is a weather fact, not a heat-island measurement, but it shows the baseline a built-up block starts from: 121°F at Pierce College in Woodland Hills on Sept. 6, 2020. [3] What I do not know # Limits of this entry The 1–7°F and 2–5°F figures are a national range from a review of studies, not a measurement of the Valley. I have not found a published heat island magnitude for a specific Valley block, and I have not measured one. If I want to claim one for a study site, I need paired temperature readings at the site and at a shaded reference, taken the same hour. Study 01 · at a glance Topanga Willows Location 4900 Topanga Canyon Blvd, Woodland Hills, Los Angeles [1] Site type Retail strip center, about 9,800 sq ft [1] Focus Heat, shade, stormwater, places to sit Methods Scaled aerial and street imagery Research review, 31 cited sources City and Caltrans rules as targets Hand-drawn plan, section, detail Status Concept study. Not commissioned by the owner. By Nathan [Last name] Date [DATE] Field guide Urban heat island Tree canopy Soil volume Permeable paving Bioswale Right-of-way 13 sections · 4 parts · 31 sources Fig. 1: the Topanga Canyon sidewalk, looking north. Showing: Proposed Concept sketch, not a rendering Today A west-facing walk with almost no shade One small street tree for a block-long row of storefronts. After noon the sun is on the paving and the glass. Proposed The same walk under a row of canopy Street trees fill the gaps, the lawn strip becomes native planting, and the storefronts get planters and a bench. Keep scrolling: the sketch has already changed. What is real here The research, the code requirements, and the layout of the site: where the building sits, the four rows of angled parking, the two driveways and the street trees are drawn from aerial imagery. [31] What is estimated Every dimension. I scaled them off the aerial, so expect them to be off by ten percent or so. The stall count (about 68), which shop is which at the south end, and where the existing seating sits are my best reading, not a survey. Part 1 of 4 The site What is there, and why it is hot 01 The site A building on the sidewalk, a parking lot behind it Topanga Willows fills the east side of Topanga Canyon Boulevard for one block, from Providencia Street down to Dumetz Road. The building is one long single-story bar, roughly 210 feet by 50, set right on the sidewalk with red awnings on both faces. [31] The owner lists it at 9,809 square feet. [1] The map shows a nail salon, a cleaner, a quilt shop, The Yoga Center and a pizza place; the owner also lists Starbucks and Yogis Grill. [1] [31] All the parking is behind the building, on the east: four rows of angled stalls on two one-way aisles, about 68 stalls, with driveways on Providencia and on Dumetz. Houses back onto the east edge. The whole lot has one small tree in it. [31] The owner counts about 30,463 vehicles a day on Topanga Canyon and 11,457 on Dumetz, with 114,413 people living within three miles. [1] A second listing gives 36,641 and 9,424, so I treat both as rough. [2] The orientation is the whole story. Because the building sits on the west side of its lot, it shades only the first row of stalls late in the day. The rest of the lot is in the sun from morning on. And the side people actually walk along, the storefronts on Topanga Canyon, faces west into the afternoon sun. One constraint: Topanga Canyon Boulevard is State Route 27, a Caltrans road. [29] The planted strip between the curb and the sidewalk is public right-of-way, so anything there is a request to the agencies, not something the owner can just build. Fig. 2: Existing conditions. Red hatching is paving in full sun. From aerial imagery Three photos this study still needs I worked from aerial and street imagery. These are the shots that would turn the estimates into evidence. Photo A Storefront sidewalk from the Dumetz corner, 3 pm, clear summer day What it would prove: That the west-facing walk is in full sun in the afternoon, which is the claim Fig. 1 rests on. Photo B The lot from the Providencia driveway at the same hour What it would prove: How far the building’s shadow really reaches, and that the other three rows get none (Fig. 2). Photo C The Dumetz corner and the one tree in the lot, with a person for scale What it would prove: Where people sit today and how small the existing canopy is, which sets the baseline for section 11. 02 The problem The hottest official reading in county history was taken a few miles from here Woodland Hills is one of the hottest parts of Los Angeles. A parking lot makes that worse in exactly the place people have to walk. 121°F Recorded at Pierce College in Woodland Hills on Sept. 6, 2020. It is the highest temperature at an official station in Los Angeles County. The old record, 119°F in 2006, was also Woodland Hills. [3] [4] 120–150°F Peak summer surface temperature of conventional paving, according to the EPA. [5] 1,500+ Extra emergency room visits in Los Angeles County on a hot day, from UCLA data reported by NBC Los Angeles. [9] NASA researchers found that heatwaves in Southern California got more frequent, more intense and longer from 1950 to 2020, with the biggest change in inland urban areas, which sit far from sea breezes and are covered in surfaces that store heat. [4] Tree canopy covers about 25 percent of the City of Los Angeles, and it is spread unevenly. [8] I do not have a canopy number for this block. Distance to Pierce College is my estimate; check it on a map.
